parsed_answer.content:
In the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) lifecycle, class loading and class initialization are distinct, sequential phases governed by the Java Language Specification. Class loading is the process of locating the binary representation of a class (typically a .class file) and creating a corresponding java.lang.Class object in the Method Area (or Metaspace in modern JVMs). This phase involves finding the class, reading the byte stream, and verifying the bytecode structure to ensure it doesn't violate JVM security constraints. It is a lazy process; the JVM does not load a class until it is actively referenced.

Class initialization, conversely, is the final stage of the class lifecycle. It occurs only after loading, linking (verification, preparation, and resolution), and specifically when the class is 'actively used'—such as invoking a static method, accessing a non-constant static field, or instantiating the class via 'new'. During initialization, the JVM executes the <clinit> method, which aggregates all static variable initializers and static blocks in the order they appear in the source code. This is where the actual state of the class is established, and it is thread-safe, protected by internal JVM locks to ensure that only one thread executes the initialization logic.

items: Loading involves the ClassLoader hierarchy (Bootstrap, Extension, Application). If a class is not found, the JVM throws a NoClassDefFoundError or ClassNotFoundException.
Preparation (part of linking) occurs between loading and initialization, where static fields are assigned default values (e.g., 0, null, false) before the <clinit> logic runs.
The <clinit> method is implicitly generated by the compiler. It is not a constructor; it is a static initializer block that runs exactly once per ClassLoader per class.
Initialization is strictly ordered. If a class has a superclass that has not been initialized, the JVM forces initialization of the superclass first.

parsed_answer.content: Beware of 'Circular Dependency' during initialization. If Class A's static block references Class B, and Class B's static block references Class A, you will likely trigger a Deadlock or an ExceptionInInitializerError. Always keep static initialization logic minimal and free of complex dependencies to avoid non-deterministic startup behavior.

title: What is the difference between class loading and class initialization?
